title: HTTP Headers & Redirect Checker | BookMyHost
description: Free HTTP headers and redirect checker: follow the redirect chain hop by hop, grade HSTS, CSP and other security headers A to F, and copy server fixes.
og_line: Follow redirects and grade security headers
answer: This tool requests a web address from our servers, follows the redirect chain by hand for up to 8 requests and grades the security headers of the final page from A to F. It flags missing HTTP to HTTPS redirects, loops, long chains and 302 redirects that should be 301, and gives copy-paste fixes for nginx, Apache and LiteSpeed.
inputs: A domain name or a full URL. A bare domain starts on plain HTTP, like a visitor typing it, so the redirect to HTTPS shows up in the chain.
outputs: Every request in the chain with status, Location and time, flags for loops, long chains and temporary redirects, the headers of the final page, a 0 to 100 score with an A to F grade, and findings with fix snippets.

p: A single address can pass through several redirects before a page loads: http to https, non-www to www, a language or login page. Browsers follow these silently. This tool follows them one request at a time, up to 8, and shows the status code, the Location header and the time for each, so you can see exactly where a visitor or a search engine ends up.

It flags a chain that never leaves plain HTTP, a loop where the chain returns to an address it already visited, a chain still redirecting after 8 requests, more than two redirects, and 302, 303 or 307 redirects that change the scheme or the host. Those changes are permanent, so a 301 or 308 is the right status.

The best chain is short. A visitor who types http://example.com should reach the final https address in one redirect, not two. Pick one canonical host name, with or without www, and send every other variant straight to it with a 301. That keeps page load fast, keeps search engines from splitting ranking between versions, and makes the security headers on the final page the only ones that matter.

Only the final page is graded, out of 100 points. Strict-Transport-Security is worth 25: a max-age of at least 15552000 seconds (180 days) earns 20, includeSubDomains adds 3 and preload adds 2. Content-Security-Policy is worth 25: 20 for an enforced policy and 5 more if it contains frame-ancestors. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff is worth 15, and clickjacking protection (X-Frame-Options DENY or SAMEORIGIN, or frame-ancestors) another 15. Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy are worth 10 each.
A is 90 or more, B 80, C 65, D 50, and anything lower is F. A final page served over plain HTTP is capped at F, because headers such as HSTS cannot protect a connection that is not encrypted.

Each missing or weak header comes with the line to add for nginx (add_header with always, inside the server block), Apache (a Header always set line in .htaccess, which needs mod_headers) and LiteSpeed, which reads the same .htaccess directive. The HTTP to HTTPS redirect and 301 fixes are shown the same way.

Add a Content-Security-Policy carefully. The starter policy blocks third-party scripts and images, so first publish it as Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only and watch what it would block. Add HSTS preload only after every subdomain works over HTTPS, since removal from browser preload lists takes months.

After changing the configuration, run the check again on the public address. A CDN or reverse proxy in front of your server can add, change or remove headers, so always test what visitors actually receive rather than what the origin server sends.
If the Server, X-Powered-By or X-AspNet-Version header shows a version number, the tool reports it as information. Hiding the number is minor hardening; updating the software matters more.

To keep the service safe, every redirect target is checked before it is requested. Private, local and internal addresses, non-web schemes and ports other than 80, 443, 8080 and 8443 are never contacted, and the chain simply stops with a note. Only the start of each response is read, and cookies are never returned. The requests come from our servers in India, so a site that redirects visitors by country may answer differently elsewhere.

faq: What is the difference between a 301 and a 302 redirect?

A 301 is permanent: browsers and search engines remember the new address. A 302 is temporary, so the old address stays in the index. Use 301 or 308 when http moves to https or one host name moves to another.
Why does the chain start on http even if I typed only a domain?
A bare domain is requested the way a visitor types it, without a scheme. That shows whether plain HTTP redirects to HTTPS. Type the full https:// address to start on HTTPS instead.
How many redirects will it follow?
Up to 8 requests. If the chain is still redirecting after that, it is flagged as too many hops, because browsers and crawlers give up on long chains.
Will it connect to internal or private addresses?

No. The address you enter and every redirect target are checked before the request, and private, loopback, link-local and other internal ranges are refused. The chain stops and the finding explains why.
Do I need every security header for an A?
No. The score is 100 points. An A needs 90, which is reachable without HSTS preload or frame-ancestors, but it needs HSTS, a Content-Security-Policy and the other four headers set well.
Does it work for LiteSpeed hosting?

Yes. LiteSpeed reads the Apache .htaccess directives, so the Header always set and RewriteRule fixes work there. On OpenLiteSpeed without .htaccess use the Header Operations setting in the WebAdmin console.
